2.text: short one paw. On the other hand, the merchants, acting as a body, were

3.text: bent on monopolizing the whole trade with the Chukchee at the yearly Anui

4.text: fair, to the exclusion of every other way and place. Thus in the year 1849

5.text: the merchants of Kolymsk entered a complaint against the Yakutsk merchant

6.text: Basile Trifonov because he wanted to re-open the disused trail to Anadyr
6.note: draft text read 'Anadvr'; the raster clearly shows 'Anadyr' (y, not v).

7.text: and Gishiga. This Trifonov was very active. He made several attempts to

8.text: find the trail. One time, guided by the official chart, he lost his way, and

9.text: returned to Omolon. On the way he visited the camps of the Chukchee and

10.text: the Lamut, and the merchants complained to the authorities that this was an

11.text: infringement of the regulations of the Anui fair.

12.text: In the year 1859 a similar complaint was entered against another merchant,

13.text: Nicholas Bereshnov, by his three cousins, Paul, Lucas, and Gabriel Bereshnov,

14.text: and it had immediate effect. I could give a long series of such examples

15.text: from the Archives of the Kolyma. Earlier than that, in the year 1834, the

16.text: Cossacks of Nishne-Kolymsk made a complaint even against the Yukaghir of

17.text: Yelombal, on the Large Anui River, because, in order to get food for them-

18.text: selves, they worked on iron and traded off the products of their work to the

19.text: Chukchee; and this was immediately forbidden.

20.text: Nevertheless, in the year 1826, the whole body of merchants complained

21.text: of the restrictions on trade. They accused the officials of having put a restraint

22.text: on trade for their own private interests, since they themselves carried on con-

23.text: siderable trade. In accordance with these complaints, the Siberian Committee,

24.text: in 1831, tried to establish free trade. The Report of the Committee points

25.text: out that because of these restrictions, the prices of imported wares are

26.text: exeedingly high. Thus tobacco, which is valued in Yakutsk at eighteen rubles
26.note: printed as set, 'exeedingly' for 'exceedingly' — printer's error, keyed verbatim per keying_spec.md §2.14.

27.text: per pud, is valued in Verkhoyansk at five rubles per pound; i. e., at more

28.text: than ten times the original price. An axe is valued at ten rubles. It is

29.text: remarkable that the permission given by the Siberian Committee for free trade

30.text: had no effect at all. On the contrary, in 1837 the order forbidding merchants

31.text: to go to the camps and settlements of the natives was reiterated. The same

32.text: was repeated several times, in 1839, 1840, 1847. The restraint was evidently

33.text: stronger than the permission to exercise freedom in trading.

34.text: Maydell’s Reform. — This condition of affairs lasted until 1859, when

35.text: Maydell repealed the regulations, and established free trade. At the same

36.text: time he tried to abolish the custom of giving to the Chukchee presents in

37.text: exchange for tribute, and to introduce a real tribute. He accomplished this,

38.text: together with a curious administrative reform in regard to the nearest groups

39.text: of the Reindeer Chukchee, while the Maritime Chukchee remained outside of

40.text: his sphere of influence. Still, in 1869 he gave no presents at the Anui fair,

41.text: not even to the Maritime traders, for their tribute. I have already spoken

42.text: of Maydell’s reform, which was based on the attempt to create official clans

43.text: for the purpose of exacting tribute; these clans were to have chiefs at the head,
